candidate_overrides.reason: YLT “the glorying of you” corresponds to ὑμετέραν (B, your). A ἡμετέραν means our. NA, WH, Byzantine and KJV-side comparisons support B; a TR minority reading has A.

YLT “with you” corresponds to μεθ’ ὑμῶν (B), not μεθ’ ἡμῶν (A, with us). Scrivener 1894 and a minority of witnesses support B; Nestle/WH/SBL and most cited early witnesses support A. Keep this as a translation-specific profile choice.

YLT “shall not be stopped” corresponds to φραγήσεται (branch B; φράσσω, stop/fence), not σφραγίζεται (branch A; seal). NA/WH/Byzantine and Scrivener-derived comparisons print φραγήσεται; one commentary notes σφραγίζεται in the TR as a possible conjecture.

YLT explicitly says “we came,” matching ἤλθομεν (B, first-person plural) rather than ἦλθον (A, third-person plural). The YLT also renders the phrase “Paul and his company”; printed editions differ in whether οἱ περὶ τὸν Παῦλον occurs together with each verb form. Scrivener 1894 gives the combination οἱ περὶ τὸν Παῦλον ἤλθομεν, while other TR/Byzantine witnesses combine the extra phrase with ἦλθον. Preserve the witness bundle; do not infer an unattested synthetic reading.

YLT “I was preaching” corresponds to ἀπήγγελλον (B, imperfect active first-person singular). Branch A ἀπαγγέλλων is a masculine nominative participle. NA/WH and Vaticanus evidence support B; TR/Byzantine tradition has A.

YLT reads “he was calling on him,” singular, matching A παρεκάλει (3rd singular imperfect). Current B παρεκάλουν is 3rd plural. Most TR editions and Byzantine text have the singular; Scrivener 1894 is an exception with the plural.

YLT “not as writing to thee” does not establish a Greek participle. A γράφω is the finite first-person verb “I write” and is syntactically natural after “I beseech thee”; English gerund phrasing is not proof of B γράφων. Do not apply B.
YLT “the court that is without the sanctuary” corresponds to ἔξωθεν (B, outside), not ἔσωθεν (A, within). NA/WH/Byzantine and the majority of listed editions support B; Scrivener TR has A.

YLT “who shalt be” corresponds to ὁ ἐσόμενος (B), not ὁ ὅσιος (A, holy). The future participle is associated with Beza/received-text tradition; major critical and Byzantine editions support ὁ ὅσιος. This is a YLT translation-profile choice, not a claim that B is the earliest reading.
YLT “I will question you something” favors the indefinite τι (B, Strong’s 5100) rather than interrogative τί (A, Strong’s 5101). Confirm the Robinson analysis and syntactic case before finalizing.

YLT “another messenger going up” corresponds naturally to present participle ἀναβαίνοντα (B), whereas A ἀναβάντα is aorist participle (“having gone up”). The critical Greek text comparison prints B. English aspect alone is not conclusive.

YLT reads “On the succeeding day, also”; branch A is τε, while current B is δέ. The YLT Greek comparison page gives Τῇ τε ἐπιούσῃ. This is a plausible YLT-profile override, but identify Young’s exact Greek source edition before finalizing.

manual_review_notes.reason: The affected token is at the beginning of the clause and substitutes tou (infinitive marker, “to turn”) with kai (“and”), not the later kai before tēs exousias. YLT “to turn [them] from darkness” supports the current A reading. The earlier apparent support for B confused this group with a different conjunction later in the verse.

The group changes ou (not) to oute (neither/nor) before metenoēsan. YLT “neither did reform” may be idiomatic English for the negative clause rather than evidence for oute. The existing rendering table does not map this YLT word to the group token. Do not override without apparatus/context review.

held_unresolved.reason: YLT “Judas also and Silas” does not uniquely decide τε versus δέ; both can be rendered with connective force. Printed editions differ (Nestle/WH/Byzantine use τε; Scrivener TR uses δέ). Retain unresolved pending source-edition identification.
YLT “and also her greatness” is compatible with the broader connective sequence; English does not isolate this particle reliably. Do not override from word matching alone.
